# **Precious metal report** _Gold, silver, platinum and palladium October 2011_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** #### **22 November 2011** #### **New York:** - October was a remarkably quiet month for price action in comparison with recent months. Gold traded “only” in a range of $150 from a low of $1,600 to a high of $1,750. In almost any other year, that would qualify as a wide monthly trading range but it was half of the distance gold moved in September. • The high price of gold and the fall in the price of silver from Q2 encouraged strong buying of silver jewellery within India during October. With Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, taking place in October this year, demand was expected to be strong anyway. Estimates by the Bombay Bullion Association are that imports of silver into India will exceed 4,000 tonnes in 2011, roughly one thousand tonnes more than last year. • NYMEX/COMEX stocks of silver and platinum are creeping higher. Typically, when physical demand for these metals is strong, material should flow from these vaults into the market. The recent increases in these stocks therefore suggest weakness in demand for both these metals, something that has been confirmed by other indicators. In part, this slow demand is likely to be seasonal but we find it a little worrying as it may also be related to the slowing world economy. In contrast, palladium stocks on NYMEX have continued to fall suggesting that the lower metal price owes more to worsening investor interest rather than fairly healthy underlying demand. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 #### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 #### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 #### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 #### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **22 November 2011** ## **Contents** |**Overview**|**3**| |---|---| |Position limits|**5**| |**Gold**

um|**24**| |Palladium production|**25**| |**Ruthenium**|**26**| 2 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **22 November 2011** ## **Overview** When one cannot remember how many previous Greek bailouts there have been, it is a sure sign of debt crisis fatigue. Nonetheless, when the latest Greek bailout was announced in late October, it finally seemed that Europe’s politicians had grasped both the importance of the situation and the market’s aversion to delay in addressing it. The response of the markets was generally positive, with some belief that a relatively positive outcome might be achievable evident. As so often, however, the first response of those in trouble is typically not to address the issue but to deny that there is an issue. The banning of short-selling of some assets and recent proposals to limit when ratings agencies could downgrade existing debt were two prime examples of this behaviour. The Greek decision to refer the bailout to referendum seemed similarly fanciful. Any referendum would have taken too long to organise to allow the next instalment of the bailout funds to be paid to keep the Greek Government functioning. Although Greek austerity is already painful, the hope that there could be a pain-free way out of the current situation is misplaced. As Argentina’s default at the start of the millennium proved, there is always significant pain within the country defaulting even if it can devalue its currency at the same time. In principle, the Greek bailout looked a fairly sensible attempt to address the current central issues in the Eurozone crisis. The decision to write down private sector-owned Greek government debt by half may not make the debt burden bearable but it is a reasonable step along the way. The additional certainty generated by this decision and the suggestion of increasing banks’ capital ratios should start to address the current crisis of liquidity in the banking system. And, the proposal to use the EFSF (European Financial system Stability Fund) effectively to insure the first slice of some member countries’ debt could, in theory reduce their costs of borrowing, helping limit contagion of other Eurozone economies. The details are, however, more problematic. Firstly, Greece is behind schedule on its deficit cutting and most commentators believe that its residual debt burden will still be too high to finance and that further “haircuts” will be required. As such, investors remain nervous about owning or buying Greek government debt and yields have risen during the first part of November rather than fallen. Italian-German 10 year bond yields (%)

The concept of recapitalising the banks too seems sensible but, unfortunately, there are two ways. Banks can go out into the marketplace to attract investment or they can cut their liabilities, restricting lending. Additionally, the banks appear to have a reasonable amount of time to comply. This means that the immediate question of stability of the financial system is not adequately addressed. Add to that, the possibility of reduced lending cutting future growth rates for an unattractive set of unintended consequences.

Finally, the leveraging of the EFSF funds in order to insure the first part of any haircut on some members’ debt is also troublesome. The structuring of the haircut on the Greek debt currently looks likely to mean that credit default swaps (CDS) are not triggered due to the “voluntary” nature of the debt forgiveness. 

One might reasonably ask whether the purchaser of a CDS might have expected to receive a pay-out on a loss of 50 per cent of the value of a bond. Investors in the bonds of the other troubled national economies should now have some of their potential losses insured for free. However, if a CDS is unlikely to pay out, they may find it impossible to insure the whole of their holdings of bonds. Conceptually, this would indicate an increase in the risk of holding the relevant bonds and there should be an additional risk premium as a result. Since the announcement, bond yields have indeed risen in some of the more atrisk European economies. 

Nonetheless, the politicians appear to have understood that action must be taken. Emergency budgets have taken place in some of the more indebted countries and it is possible that the foundations are slowly being put into place for a more stable system. Our expectation is that Greece will not leave the Euro and that the debt crisis will gradually be resolved without a set of disorderly defaults. However, this process will be neither smooth nor speedy. We expect default risk to continue to be priced into the market for some time to come. It is also clear that the previous bargain of 2-3 per cent growth and 1-2 per cent inflation could well be reversed for the next few years within Europe as a result of this wave of austerity. We feel that economic growth may struggle to reach 2 per cent per annum and that inflation could be higher for an extended period. 

This would tend to argue for lower demand for the more industrial of the precious metals but high sustained demand for gold in the medium term. This suggests that there is scope still for gold to outperform the other precious metals. However, in the short term at least, further pressure on the Euro can be expected, with any rise in the price of gold (in Dollar terms) perhaps being delayed until the current bout of Euro selling subsides.

**_Figure 3_** _: Although the purchasing manager index remains above 50, indicating a growing US economy, the downwards trend it shows is worrying._ Looking at North America, the US economy is sending some mixed signals. While unemployment remains high and house sales remain depressed, the purchasing manager index remains in positive territory, suggesting that the economy is still growing even though there is a clear downwards trend in business confidence. Growth rates are anaemic and little sense exists of a robust economy. However, our belief is that, although significant risks remain in the world economy, global GDP growth can be expected next year and that there may be some gradual reduction in the risk of a further financial market crisis later this year or in 2012. Our view on the outlook for the precious metals is therefore generally still for higher prices next year. ### **Position limits** During October, the CFTC (Commodities Futures Trading Commission) voted to impose position limits on a range of commodities in an effort to reduce the exposure of these commodities to speculative interest. COMEX and NYMEX precious metals contracts are affected. All commodities will be treated similarly with spot month contract position limits for one entity apparently to be limited to 25 per cent of deliverable supply. Later month positions will be subject to ten per cent of the first 25,000 contracts and 2.5 per cent of any further open interest above that level. As far as we can tell, according to Appendix A attached to the final rule (http:// www.cftc.gov/ucm/groups/public/@newsroom/documents/file/federalregister101811c.pdf, p259), spot month limits should be 3,000 contracts for gold, 1,500 contracts for silver and 650 and 500 respectively for palladium and platinum). Given that the specific intention behind the introd

uction of these new position limits is to deter “excessive” speculation, when they take effect we can expect there to be some market impact, although precisely what that might be is hard to predict. 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **22 November 2011** ## **Gold** A key question in the gold market is whether the move above $1,900 was a short term blip or a real peak driven by market fundamentals. If $1,900 per ounce and above were “real” prices, then gold’s weakness from mid-September to the end of October was somewhat mystifying. If, on the other hand, this was merely a short term market distortion, the bull trend for gold remains entirely intact and, with market risk still disturbingly high, gold has the potential to push on to $2,000. In either case, October was a remarkably quiet month for price action in comparison with recent months. Gold traded “only” in a range of $150 from a low of $1,600 to a high of $1,750. In almost any other year, that would qualify as a wide monthly trading range but it was half of the distance gold moved in September. While the US Dollar had strengthened during September, it weakened throughout most of October, allowing gold and other commodity prices to rise in Dollar terms. The initial moves were part of the rebound from the brief dip below $1,600 in late September and saw gold carried to roughly $1,680 by mid-month despite a lack of Chinese buying during the October Golden Week holidays. Later, the Chinese buyers returned and Indian physical purchasing intensified ahead of Diwali. Gold Price(USD/oz)

**_Figure 4_** _: Despite a clear increase in macroeconomic risk, the gold price has struggled to approach its earlier highs in recent weeks._ Interestingly, once again aligned itself with equities and when weak Chinese GDP data was released on the 17th , gold fell back alongside equities, finally stopping at a low of $1,605 on the 20th . Slowly, confidence started to build that European political leaders might finally be able to start moving towards a solution to the widespread debt crisis. This firmed the Euro against the Dollar, sending commodities higher with gold climbing steadily to $1,660 on the 25th . Later that day, it leapt through the $1,700 barrier as risk-off trades became the order of the day and a number of stops were triggered. Gold kept rising and reached $1,720 on the 27th . The latest European rescue plan was announced and the Euro strengthened in what seemed even at the time an overoptimistic response by the markets. Gold stepped up to touch a monthly high of $1,750 on the 28th . This optimism slowly started to leak away and the Dollar bounced against m

ost currencies, aided by the Japanese Ministry of Finance’s intervention to weaken the Yen, and gold softened to end the month close to $1,720.

### **Mining costs** 

At its latest results presentation, Barrick indicated that its costs were expected to climb by close to ten per cent in 2012, largely due to wage inflation. Wage rises were running by roughly 20 per cent in Argentina and roughly 8 per cent elsewhere in South America. The imposition of higher mining royalties by a number of jurisdictions is also set to have an inflationary effect. (For interest 2011 and 2012 production forecasts are for roughly 7.6 to 7.8 million ounces although there are plans to boost this to 9 million ounces per year by 2016.) 

Typical current cash costs within the industry are roughly $600 per ounce of gold extracted. Including exploration costs or looking at the costs of new mines coming on-stream moves that figure substantially higher. However, unlike in the platinum market, rising costs, while an issue, do not currently provide any significant floor for the gold price. 

### **Indian jewellery demand** 

Indian jewellery sales remain highly seasonal so the recent Diwali festival which took place in October was an important marker for the health of the industry. A high gold price meant that sales were lower in volume terms than a year earlier, although they were higher in value terms. However, the fall in the gold price prior to the start of the festival (compared to the recent all-time highs) seems to have rejuvenated the interest of many consumers, suggesting that the Indian behaviour of buying on the dips remains in place even at today’s high prices. 

According to the Bombay Bullion Association, “People have burnt their fingers in the stock market and property is gradually slipping from reach. They are coming home to gold, as it were.” For the year as a whole, gold imports into India look as if they could reach one thousand tonnes, stronger than in 2010 (958 tonnes) despite a substantially higher price. 

### **Other developing countries: Vietnam and Turkey** 

The stress in the global financial system and gold’s pseudo-currency role were confirmed by activities in Vietnam where the central bank is looking to tighten controls on the domestic gold market including the import and export of gold bullion. The gold market has become increasingly problematic as inflation soars and the government tries to control the foreign exchange market. A shortage of US Dollars has developed with many of these Dollars being used to buy gold or pay foreign currency loans and the Government is trying to control both Dollar and gold trading in order to support its currency at its current official exchange rate. 

In Turkey, the Central Bank was forced to intervene in the currency markets to support the lira which had weakened buy roughly twenty per cent against the US Dollar. Amon

gst the actions taken was a decision to increase the maximum portion of the required reserve ratio with domestic banks must keep with the Central Bank. There is also a proposal to allow up to ten per cent of these reserves to be held in the form of gold, something that should encourage more gold demand. ### **Gold investment** In late October, the Royal Canadian Mint announced its plans to offer Exchange Traded Receipts in gold. Each receipt is roughly equivalent to a London Metal Exchange (LME) warrant. They can be traded but they give the holder the ownership of an amount of gold in the mint’s vaults. As such, they are an allocated product and any investment in them will contribute to physical demand. The initial offer is expected to close in November and to reach CAD250 million, or 140,000 ounces of metal. In the current climate, where investors are worried about the stability of banks and many have therefore chosen to invest in allocated or physical material, we expect this offer to be fully subscribed and we would not be surprised to see further offerings in the short to medium term. 7 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **22 November 2011** Meanwhile, ETF buying accelerated during October. We have previously noted that some risk fatigue has set into this market, as has been seen in the gold coin market. Once an investor has purchased some gold as insurance, the safe haven aspect of gold should become less attractive. Six month rolling US Mint gold coin sales (oz)

**_Figure 7_** _:Negative COMEX flows have stopped for the moment at least but renewed buying interest has been a little disappointing_ One final interesting angle for gold investors comes from a few recent news stories of investors starting to favour gold mining equities over gold as an investment. Logically, this should only be an attractive trade to those investing in gold in order to make a return rather than due to risk aversion or from a desire to diversify their asset holdings. However, if an investor expects the gold price to slow in its upwards movement and some stability to return to equity markets, this could make gold equities the more attractive investment. Barrick, Kinross, Newmont and Yamana Gold have all either initiated or grown their dividends in recent months. We do not expect the risk premium to disappear from the gold price quickly given the severity of the current Eurozone debt crisis but the alternative of investing in a dividendpaying equity based on gold might gradually start to erode investor interest in the metal itself. ### **China** Sales of gold on the Shanghai Gold Exchange continue to head towards an annual record total. According to the World Gold Council’s estimates, demand within China could rise by ten per cent in 2011 compared to a year earlier. **_Figure 9_** _:The interplay between interest rates and inflation is an important factor in consumer sentiment towards gold._ With inflation decreasing and – possibly – being under control, there could be less incentive for Chinese consumers to buy metal in the next few months. However, official CPI is still significantly higher than deposit rates and real CPI may well be above official banking sector lending rates. In this environment, and with the gold price rising, we feel that Chinese buying of gold is likely to continue at an elevated pace. ### **Gold demand trends** According to the World Gold Council’s (WGC) most recent Gold Demand Trends quarterly report, gold demand for Q3 2011 was 6 per cent up on Q3 2010 at 1,054 tonnes. Supply rose by 2 per cent to 1034 tonnes, meaning that the market appears to be in deficit. Looking at demand in more detail, the WGC notes that jewellery demand was down by 10 per cent on one year earlier at 466 tonnes, with a fall in Indian purchasing the main reason for this weakness. Usage in industrial applications was almost unchanged at 120 tonnes despite high prices (which often drive some demand elasticity) while investment demand climbed by a third from 352 tonnes to 468 tonnes, pushing the market into a deficit. In the jewellery sector, the recent weakness of the Rupee has been hurting Indian jewellery demand. High metal prices have also had a negative effect and the only national markets which recorded year-on-year growth in Q3 were China, Hong Kong, Japan and Russia. Indian demand fell 26 per cent. Chinese jewellery demand in Q3 was higher than Indian demand. This is only the fourth quarter since the start of 2003 that Chinese jewellery demand has been higher than Indian jewellery demand (the Renminbi strengthened against the Dollar instead of weakening, helping support demand within China). Chinese total demand (i.e. not just jewellery demand) for the first three quarters of 2011 was already stronger than demand for the full year in 2010. India will remain the largest market in the world but China is continuing to close this gap. Indian year-to-date demand is close to where it was last year and annual demand could reach 960 tonnes to 1,000 tonnes. Looking forwards, the World Gold Council (WGC) does not expect a decline in the size of these markets but does believe that the rate of growth will slow. 10 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **22 November 2011** In investment, physical bar demand and coin demand climbed by about a third each to 294 tonnes and 76 tonnes respectively. ETF investment was strong too, climbing 58 per cent to 78 tonnes, split evenly between North America and Europe. The WGC believes that there was OTC selling of about 37 tonnes during the quarte

r. In the physical market, European demand was more than twice as large as in Q3 2010 with Europe now the largest market, reflecting the Eurozone crisis issues and consumers’ fear-based response to them. 

Electronics industry use of gold actually rose during Q3 2011 compared to Q2 as is often the case with demand typically seasonally strong in the lead-up to Christmas. Year-onyear though, there was little change in demand even though some of these industrial applications typically show sensitivity to high prices with demand falling when prices rise. 

On the supply side, mine production climbed 5 per cent to 746 tonnes. Recycling climbed by 13 per cent to 427 tonnes, a strong response to the record prices (although this total was lower than, for instance in Q4 2010, demonstrating that recycling is not simply driven by high metal prices). There was a net 10 tonnes of hedging compared to 54 tonnes of dehedging in Q3 2010 with almost all of this hedging being undertaken for project finance purposes. 

The official sector was again a buyer of gold in Q3 2011 as it has been for the last two years. Looking back a few years, it typically sold 400 tonnes of gold or thereabouts per year, so the switch to buying behaviour is an important one and has now become wellestablished. 50 tonnes of Q3 purchasing was identified during the quarter (from countries including Russia, Bolivia, Mexico etc.) but there is roughly 100 tonnes of central bank purchasing which was not identified. The WGC believes this is composed of buying from multiple central banks and believes that these should be based in countries which are running surpluses which would identify the likely culprits as South American, Far East or Central Asian banks. Given the scale of the buying, market sentiment will assume that much of this buying is by the Chinese state.

## **<mark>Silver</mark>** 

Silver combined a dogged desire to follow gold with a wild streak that led to wide price movements. Having fallen to $26 in late September, little more than half of its April highs, October was an opportunity to rebuild investor morale. Europe was the focus rather than anything specifically related to the silver market itself and the ebb and flow of sentiment over Greece and the other significant debtors. As gold soared later in the month, silver followed, climbing to end the month near $34, a reasonably positive performance compared to the previous month. 



**_Figure 10_** _: The recovery in the silver price during October was somewhat unconvincing._ 

Looking over the last few months reinforces the view that the price of silver has been drive by factors external to the silver market. Since May, the palladium and silver prices have moved in concert, suggesting that both metals are being viewed as a cross between an industrial material and a precious metal by investors.

**_Figure 12_** _: However, typical price seasonality trends suggest that the silver price could appreciate during the final months of 2011._ ### **Indian silver jewellery** The high price of gold and the fall in the price of silver from Q2 encouraged strong buying of silver jewellery within India during October. With Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, taking place in October this year, demand was expected to be strong anyway. Estimates by the Bombay Bullion Association are that imports of silver into India will exceed 4,000 tonnes in 2011, roughly one thousand tonnes more than last year. Strong silver demand is typically symptomatic of lower levels of business being transacted in the gold market as precious metal traders look to silver to augment their softer gold sales. ### **Solar cells and industrial demand** The solar industry’s soft sales continued through the third quarter of 2011 although we expect to see further growth from this industry in 2012. However, the short term picture remains somewhat negative. The UK is only the latest European country to cut government subsidies to individuals installing solar cells. As was seen elsewhere, the UK indicated that the cut in feed-in tariffs (the amount of money received for selling solar power back into the electrical grid) was due to the fall in solar panel costs. In part, this is true but the European drive to austerity is another driving force. With many governments being forced to cut costs, programmes such as these solar power subsidy schemes will suffer more in the next year or two. However, at the same time as Europe has retreated from the vanguard of installing solar power, China and California have become more prominent. China’s release of a national feed-in tariff for solar power during July 2011 has led to a rush of project activity within the country. Although it will take a period of time for these projects to start being installed, this should mean that solar demand, and hence demand for silver, should improve next year. Other industrial sectors, such as the electronics industry, are healthier this year and are taking good amounts of silver. Overall, though, physical silver demand appears to have weakened during the second half of

**_Figure 13_** _: Rising COMEX stocks are a worrying indicator of softer end user silver demand._ **Silver investment** The Shanghai Futures Exchange has revealed that it plans to launch a silver futures contract in the first half of 2012. Currently, the only futures-like contract available within China is the silver T+D deferred contract traded on the Shanghai Gold Exchange. The addition of a pure futures contract should encourage further trading within China and is a valuable step towards the regularisation of metals trading within China. However, we would urge some caution in that the equivalent gold contract has, to date, been used extensively for simple speculation as well as hedging. While this is similar to the situation on COMEX and TOCOM, the extreme daily changes in buying or selling interest on the Chinese exchanges suggest that the introduction of this contract could contribute towards higher short term price volatility in the silver market in times of market stress than would otherwise be the case. We note that the gold-platinum spread remained over $100 and seems to indicate at least a degree of scepticism over the likelihood of a controlled solution to the Eurozone debt crisis being found. ### **The Chinese platinum jewellery market** The economics 101 view of the platinum jewellery market assumes that as the platinum price approaches that of gold, platinum jewellery sales increase dramatically. Throughout most of the world, platinum jewellery has higher mark-ups than gold (for a range of reasons) at a retail level. So, although the metal prices may be close to one another, this does not mean that the prices of similar pieces of finished jewellery of either metal have approached one another. In the short term, the relative price movements should, though make gold relatively more expensive and, in a normal world, less attractive to consumers. Additionally, platinum should offer higher potential profits for the jewellery industry and we should see consumer pull and retailer/manufacturer push assist platinum demand. To an extent this has happened. In China, however, retail and manufacturer mark-ups are relatively modest and turnover is a very important component of profitability. With other investments unattractive for various reasons (an underperforming stock market, limits on house

ownership and so on), a rising gold price has attracted strong buying interest into this metal. This has encouraged the devotion of more space at the retailer, and capacity at the manufacturer, to gold jewellery. So, although we have seen a response in platinum demand, this has been rather more modest than might have been expected. We do not feel that a few months of gold trading at a premium to platinum would have any impact on platinum’s attractiveness as the premium “brand” but we do feel that further capacity expansions could occur throughout the industry which could allow an increased uptake of platinum through the start of 2012. Interestingly, September sales themselves were marginally up compared to September 2010. Portuguese, Spanish, Irish and Italian buyers proved less keen on buying new vehicles than they had been one year earlier as austerity continues to bite. Interestingly, more cars were sold in the smaller Greek market than in September 2010 although year-to-date sales are one third down on the first nine months of last year. However, it is worth noting that European Union car sales fell 1.8 per cent year-on-year in October: the downturn is not over yet. Within this, fleet car sales have become more important in supporting European new car demand and, in particular demand for diesel vehicles. Within the UK, for instance, September sales were 0.7 per cent lower than in September 2020. However, private car buying slipped by over 9 per cent to only 47 per cent of the total market. Over half of the vehicles purchased were bought either as fleet cars or directly by businesses. Fleet sales actually rose and, as a result, while the number of gasoline-fuelled cars sold in the first three quarters of the year fell from 890,000 units in 2010 to 759,000 units in 2011, the number of diesel cars rose by 6.4 per cent, climbing from 728,000 units to 774,000 units even in a weak market. ### **Fuel cells** Automotive fuel cells edged back into the headlines during October, if only briefly. Nissan announced that it has developed a new fuel cell stack (effectively a fuel cell “engine”) which uses only a quarter of the amount of platinum used in its 2005 model and

which is substantially cheaper all round. We have not seen full details of how this thrifting has been achieved or of the metal loadings concerned but we estimate that this would give a fuel cell stack with a metal content of between 10 and 20g (and probably towards the higher end of that range). 

This thrifting process is **_positive_** for platinum demand. At current prices, an ounce of platinum costs roughly $1,650. Any fuel cell vehicle which contained more than an ounce of platinum could not hope to be cost-competitive with current technologies. With the platinum representing a significant part of the cost of a fuel cell, reduction in the amount of metal used is the only route to potential widespread commercialisation. Thrifting is therefore an essential part of product development to allow the technology a chance to succeed. 

The latest annual review from Fuel Cell Today (www.fuelcelltoday.com) notes that a number of car manufacturers are planning to launch limited runs of fuel cell cars by 2015 which could lead to sales of 20,000 vehicles globally. We would urge some caution, having worked in the fuel cell industry for almost ten years. Fuel cell commercialisation dates have been missed regularly by the automotive sector since the start of the millennium. However, Fuel Cell Today does see some signs of improving commercial prospects in non-automotive applications and demand should start to increase organically. We still do not see fuel cells as the next major demand growth story but note that they could readily contribute several tens of thousands of ounces of demand per year before the end of the current decade.

With iridium crucibles widely used in the production of LEDs, any slowdown will also be negative for iridium demand. We also note that NYMEX platinum stocks have once again been growing, having previously been falling from their global economic crisis high in 2008/2009. These tend to rise at times of low demand elsewhere and are a signifier of weak demand. We are not overly bearish on the outlook for the global economy and expect automotive and industrial demand to continue at respectable levels next year. However, until we see a reduction in these stocks, we cannot be completely convinced that this current price weakness is solely due to seasonality and the normal cyclical behaviour of demand in the glass and chemical sectors. Impala came to a two year agreement with the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM). This will see wages increasing by between 8 and 10 per cent in each year. Although these increases are considerably above the current level of inflation, they are substantially below the initial union claim of 14 per cent, adding to cost pressures at the mines. Other companies have typically agreed wage rises of similar size. However, discussions are still continuing at Northam and there have been week-long strikes over wages at Smokey Hills (Platinum Australia), over union recognition at Everest and at Xstrata’s operations over the proposed introduction of a share ownership scheme for employees. While the wage question has almost been settled for the year, the fractious industrial relations climate is becoming increasingly clear to any casual observer. However, imports, often of luxury vehicles made in Europe, grew once again, driving palladium demand upwards at a greater speed. Chinese manufacturers also increased their efforts to export their products with these growing by fifty per cent year-on-year to an expected record 800,000 units for the whole year. Fortunately, reports from car dealers suggest that sticker prices have not changed following the end of these eco-car subsidies and that demand for these smaller vehicles has remained relatively robust so far. October passenger car production climbed 5 per cent on October 2010 to 1.25 million units while sales were 1.22 million units, one per cent more than a year earlier. It is important to note that month-on-month comparisons between September and October are unhelpful as October normally features the National Day/Golden Week holidays, when few vehicle sales take place. Looking further forward into the future, recent forecasts by China’s National Development and Reform Commission indicate that Chinese domestic light duty vehicle production capacity could exceed 30 million units per year by 2015. When put in the context of a current global market of roughly 80 million units, this shows the scale of the expansion still expected by some in this key market. North American vehicle sales continue to improve despite a rather flabby economy. October car sales reached 489.000 units in the USA, five per cent higher than a year earlier. Truck sales climbed by 10 per cent to 532,000 units, suggesting that, in the absence of a further economic downturn, the industry may slowly be moving back towards healthier levels of sales and higher palladium and rhodium demand. Elsewhere, growth is expected to moderate in the Russian market, falling from 30 per cent to a still healthy 12 per cent. This should see Russian car sal

es return to pre-crisis levels. In a rather unwelcome reminder of the fragility of the global supply chain for the automotive market, the extraordinary floods in Thailand have started to have a negative impact on the Japanese carmakers. Although this is likely to be a relatively short term issue, Honda has cut back its European production marginally and its North American output was temporarily cut by half in late October; Toyota has started to trim some of its US production. While we expect the effect on platinum group metal demand to be limited, this does illustrate the challenge that the Japanese producers face in catching up their lost output from Q2 and Q3. ### **Automotive regulations** An interesting note on European automotive emissions regulations has emerged recently in which the European Commission has started to consult with stakeholders over forthcoming EU 6/EU VI emissions rules. One specific suggestion is the desire to tighten emissions limits for cold starts (below 7 degrees C). ## **<mark>Ruthenium</mark>** 

Ruthenium does not feature frequently in the wider precious metals markets. However, we note an interesting Reuters story from October which pointed out that the Zhejiang Gold and Silver Products Market (not the largest exchange within China admittedly) has launched a ruthenium contract to allow retail customers to invest/speculate in this metal. 

We have heard of informal investment in a range of other exotic materials such as indium (and seen this within China on our previous visits) and feel that this shows the speculative frenzy that can take place in the metals markets in China on occasion. This was wellillustrated by a comment in the Reuters article from a customer service representative at this exchange: Who would want to take physical gold? People just want to speculate on price moves and make a profit.” Although we believe, as with Vietnam, that Government control of the gold market and the limited convertibility of the local currency make gold an attractive investment, this enhanced degree of speculative interest can onl

y be expected to contribute extra volatility to the metals markets globally, particularly if it leads to further interest in the less liquid minor metals.
